title: The falls that went under
teaches: The Columbia turned into a stair of reservoirs, and Celilo Falls drowned in 1957
summary: **Celilo Falls was a fishing place for thousands of years.** The whole Columbia poured over a basalt ledge there, and people fished it with dip nets from wooden platforms until 1957; salmon bones at Five Mile Rapids nearby are about ten thousand years old.
**A falls is a difference in level.** What you see as a falls is how far the water above the ledge stands over the water below, so anything that raises the water below shrinks it.
**Backwater shrank Celilo every June.** In the snowmelt flood the river piled up behind the Long Narrows downstream, and in big years the water below rose almost to the water above.
**A reservoir is nearly flat.** Its water stands at about the dam's height until the river's own bed climbs above it, which is how a dam 15 km downstream drowned the falls on 10 March 1957.

**The Columbia is now a stair of lakes.** Eleven dams on the river in the United States turn its drop into steps, and of about 960 km above the tide only the Hanford Reach, about 80 km, still runs free.
**Most of the dams pass the river straight through.** Run-of-the-river dams hold only days of flow; storage dams, Grand Coulee and the dams in Canada and on tributaries, can hold back weeks of it.
**Storage flattens the year.** Water held back from the June snowmelt is let out in autumn and winter, so the river now runs lower in June and higher in winter than it did.
**Grand Coulee stopped the salmon.** Built far too tall for a fish ladder, it ended the salmon runs to the upper Columbia and Canada.

blocks.text: About 20 km upstream of the town of The Dalles, Oregon, the Columbia used to fall over a ledge of black basalt. It was all of the river at once: the water gathered from British Columbia, Montana, Idaho and most of Washington and Oregon, dropping into a jumble of channels and eddies cut in the rock. The people who lived beside it called the falls Wyam. Most maps called them Celilo Falls.

Salmon heading upriver to spawn had to get past the falls, and they gathered in the eddies below them to rest before they tried. Fishers stood on wooden platforms built out over the white water and swept long-handled dip nets through those eddies. How long people have fished here is told by a dig at Five Mile Rapids, a few kilometres downstream of the falls, where salmon bones lie in layers about ten thousand years old. Celilo itself was a fishing and trading place for the peoples of the river for as long as anyone's records and stories reach.[^treaty]

In 1855 the Yakama, the Warm Springs, the Umatilla and the Nez Perce nations signed treaties with the United States. They gave up most of their land, and the treaties promised in writing that they kept the right to fish "at all usual and accustomed places": wherever they had always fished, on or off their reservations. Celilo was the best known of those places. A century later it was still fished the same way, from platforms, with dip nets, by families who had fished it for generations.

On 10 March 1957 the Army Corps of Engineers closed the gates of The Dalles Dam, which stands just upstream of the town and about 15 km downstream of the falls. Crowds gathered on the banks to watch, many of them families who fished there. Through the day the water below the falls rose to meet the water above, the noise of the falls faded, and by evening Celilo was under a lake.

Two things about this are puzzling. The dam was 15 km away, yet it drowned the falls in a day. And the falls had a habit of shrinking every summer, long before any dam was built. The second puzzle is the place to start, and it answers the first.

parts.title: A falls that shrank every June

blocks.text: Lesson 2 (floods) drew a river's year as a hydrograph, its discharge against time. The Columbia's year at The Dalles had one great swell in it. Through autumn and winter the river ran low, because most of the basin's winter precipitation fell as snow on the Rockies and the Cascades and stayed there. In April the snow began to melt, and by June the river carried five or six times its winter flow. The snowmelt flood of late spring is called the **freshet**.

At low water, in autumn, the river dropped several metres over the ledge at Celilo, around 6 m (20 feet) by most accounts. In the freshet the drop shrank, and in a big year it all but vanished for weeks. The reason was downstream. A few kilometres below the falls the whole river had to squeeze through the Long Narrows, also called Five Mile Rapids, a slot of basalt far narrower than the river's usual width; the town of The Dalles is named for these rapids. A narrow slot passes a small flow easily, but a big flow has to pile up behind it until it is deep enough to push through, so in June the river below the falls rose many metres.

The river above the falls rose much less. Its level was set by the ledge itself: water spilling over a lip only has to rise a little to pass a lot more flow. So in a big freshet the water below climbed toward the water above, and the step between them shrank.

blocks.caption: Celilo Falls in three states: at low water, with a fishing platform and dip net over the eddy below; in the June flood, when backwater from the Long Narrows raised the river below; and since 1957, under Lake Celilo. Compare the height of the step in each.

blocks.text: A falls is a difference in level: how far the surface above the ledge stands over the surface below it. Raise the water below and the falls shrinks, however high the river is above the sea. Water raised by an obstruction downstream is called **backwater**,[^backwater] and backwater from the narrows shrank Celilo for part of every year. A dam raises backwater too, and keeps it there all year.

From the Canadian border to the sea the Columbia runs about 1,200 km and falls about 400 m (1,300 feet), the height of its water surface at the border. Water falling that far carries a great deal of energy, and from the 1930s the Corps, the Bureau of Reclamation and public utilities built dams to turn the fall into electricity. Each dam holds the river up at its face, and its lake reaches back upstream. A lake's surface is nearly flat, so the raised water stands at about the dam's height until the riverbed climbs above it. The Dalles Dam held the river some 25 m (80 feet) higher at its face, and its lake, Lake Celilo, reached back almost 40 km. The falls, 15 km up, were well inside it. That answers the first puzzle.

Put enough dams in a row and each lake reaches back to the foot of the next dam. The river becomes a stair: flat treads of still water, with the whole drop taken in steps at the dams, where it turns the turbines.[^power] Eleven dams now stand on the Columbia between the border and the tide, the lowest of them Bonneville. The figure adds them in the years they filled, and the slider under it runs through the years from 1930 to 1975.

blocks.caption: The Columbia from the sea to the Canadian border, as the dams went in, drawn as height against distance. The heights are stretched about 1,400 times against the distances, so the steps look like cliffs; really the river slopes gently. Pool heights are rounded, and the river between dam sites is drawn as a straight slope, so the old falls at Celilo is marked with a dot.
blocks.task: Guess how much of the river above the tide still runs free, then play the years to 1975

blocks.text: Bonneville, in the Columbia Gorge, came first of the big dams, in 1938, and was built with fish ladders: staircases of pools that salmon can climb one pool at a time.[^ladders] Grand Coulee, finished in 1942, is the tallest step, about 100 m from its lake down to the river below, and the largest power station in the United States. A ladder that high was beyond anything built then, and Grand Coulee was built with no way for salmon to pass. The runs to the upper Columbia and into Canada ended there. Its lake, Lake Roosevelt, runs about 240 km back to the border, and as it filled it drowned Kettle Falls, another great fishing place of the upper river.[^kettle]

The Snake, the Columbia's biggest tributary, joins it at the Tri-Cities, inside the lake behind McNary Dam. By 1968, when John Day Dam filled the last gap between the Gorge and the Snake, the treads met almost everywhere. Of the roughly 960 km of the Columbia above the tide in the United States, the only stretch still running as a river is the Hanford Reach, about 80 km between Priest Rapids Dam and the head of the lake behind McNary. The dams on the Snake and in Canada are not drawn here; they are steps on the same stair.

parts.title: What a dam does to the year

blocks.text: Most of the dams on the stair hardly change how much water goes down the river. Bonneville, The Dalles, John Day and McNary are **run-of-the-river** dams: their lakes are long but shallow for the flow they carry, holding only days of the river's water, so what comes in at the top goes out through the turbines at about the same rate. They change the river's levels and its speed, and they drowned its falls and rapids, but not its year.

A **storage** dam is different. Grand Coulee, the three dams Canada built in the 1960s and 1970s, and tall dams on tributaries in Montana and Idaho have deep lakes that can be drawn down by tens of metres and filled again. Together they hold back water in spring and let it out later in the year. The figure's slider sets how much they hold back; before moving it, think about what that has to do to the hydrograph at The Dalles.

blocks.caption: A typical year at The Dalles, before the dams (dashed, a model rounded from monthly means of the old record) and with water held back in spring and let out in autumn and winter (purple, the colour used for dams and levees in every figure). Water held back is shaded blue; water let out later is shaded purple.
blocks.task: Guess, then hold back 20 km³, about what the dams hold back in an ordinary year

blocks.text: Every cubic metre held back in June has to come out some time, and it comes out when the river is low. The storage lakes are drawn down through autumn and winter, when the Northwest uses the most electricity, and they are lowest in early spring, which leaves room to catch the next freshet. So the regulated river runs lower in June and higher in winter than the river it replaced.

Full to empty, all the storage lakes together hold about 50 km³, a third of the river's flow in a year at The Dalles. In an ordinary year they shift about 20 km³ from spring to winter, less than half of what they could, because some room is kept empty for a big flood and some water is kept for dry years, for power and for fish.

The flattened year matters to salmon too. Young salmon heading to sea used to ride the freshet down a fast river; now they cross a string of slow lakes, and each spring part of the flow is let out over the dams' **spillways**, the open gates that pass water over or beside a dam without going through the turbines, to carry them past. What happens to the fish themselves belongs to another course. The next lesson, Vanport (C2), takes the same storage from the other side: what it does to a flood.

Celilo Village, on the bank above where the falls were, is still home to a small community, and a salmon feast is still held there each spring. In the 1950s the government paid the four treaty nations for the loss of the fishery. Treaty fishing goes on along the river, from platforms, boats and nets, at other sites the tribes still use.

The falls are under still water, not gone: the basalt ledge is down there, under Lake Celilo. If The Dalles Dam were ever taken down, the river would fall over it again, as the Elwha began to run through its old canyon in lesson 4 (sediment) once its two dams came out.

blocks.caption: Six questions on Celilo and the dams
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Long before any dam, Celilo Falls nearly vanished in a big June flood. Which explanation is best?
choices: Narrow rapids downstream backed the river up, so the water below rose far more than above
The flood scoured the ledge each June, so the falls wore lower every spring before the rock re-formed
The water above the falls rose so far in June that it spread over the banks around the ledge instead
items.why: A falls is the difference between the level above and the level below. Behind the Long Narrows a big flow piled up, raising the river below Celilo, while the river above, set by the ledge, rose much less.

items.ask: The Dalles Dam stood about 15 km downstream of Celilo Falls, yet its lake covered them within a day. Why?
choices: Its lake surface is nearly flat, so it stays near the dam's height for tens of km
The dam's lake filled with fresh snowmelt that was arriving from upstream that week
The slowed river dropped its sand at once, and the sand built up over the ledge
items.why: The dam held the river about 25 m higher at its face. Still water lies level, so that height reached back almost 40 km, well past the falls.

items.ask: What do storage reservoirs on the Columbia do to the river's year at The Dalles?
choices: Lower the June peak and raise the winter flow
Lower the winter flow to save water for the June turbines
Raise the June peak by releasing their stored water early
items.why: Water held back from the June snowmelt is let out in autumn and winter, when the river is low and electricity is most needed. The lakes shift water from one season to another.

items.ask: Bonneville and The Dalles are run-of-the-river dams. What does that mean for the river below them?
choices: Its yearly pattern of high and low flow is hardly changed
Its flow is held steady all year at the yearly average
Its spring peak is cut, because each lake fills in June
items.why: Their lakes hold only days of flow, so water leaves about as fast as it arrives. They raise the level and slow the river, but shifting water between seasons takes the storage dams upstream.

items.ask: Of about 960 km of the Columbia above the tide in the United States, how much still runs free of a reservoir?
choices: About 240 km, the stretch below Grand Coulee
About 400 km, from McNary up to Grand Coulee
items.why: Each dam's lake reaches back to the foot of the next. Only the Hanford Reach, between Priest Rapids Dam and the head of McNary's lake, still runs as a river.

items.ask: Why did Grand Coulee end the salmon runs to the upper Columbia when Bonneville did not?
choices: It had no fish ladder: its 100 m step was far too tall
Its lake grew too warm in summer for salmon to cross it
Its turbines killed every salmon that passed through them
items.why: Bonneville was built with fish ladders in 1938. Grand Coulee, about 100 m from lake to river, was built with no way past, and the runs above it ended.

treaty.title: Trade at the falls
treaty.text: Fish caught at Celilo were dried and pounded and traded far up and down the river and across the plateau, and the falls drew people from a great distance in the fishing season. Lewis and Clark passed the falls in October 1805 and wrote about the crowds of fishers and the stacks of dried fish.

backwater.title: Backwater
backwater.text: Anything that slows a river from downstream, a narrows, a dam, a high tide at the mouth, or a bigger river at a junction, makes the water stand higher upstream of it. Hydrologists call the raised water backwater. It fades upstream, and it stops at a falls or a steep riffle, where the water runs fast enough that the raised level below can't reach back over it, until the water below climbs nearly to the lip.

power.title: Height and flow make power
power.text: The power in falling water is the weight of water falling each second times the height it falls. A cubic metre of water weighs about 1,000 kg, so with a flow of Q cubic metres a second dropping h metres the power is about 1,000 × 9.8 × Q × h watts. Grand Coulee's flow of about 3,000 m³/s falling about 100 m gives 1,000 × 9.8 × 3,000 × 100 ≈ 3 billion watts, from one dam. The same flow through a 25 m step gives a quarter of that.

ladders.title: Fish ladders
ladders.text: A fish ladder is a staircase of pools, each a little higher than the last, with water running down it so salmon can swim and leap up one pool at a time. Visitors at Bonneville can watch salmon pass windows beside the ladders. A ladder that climbed 100 m would have run for kilometres, and nothing like it had been built when Grand Coulee went up.

kettle.title: Kettle Falls
kettle.text: Kettle Falls, near the town of the same name in northeastern Washington, was the great fishing place of the upper Columbia. It went under Lake Roosevelt in 1940, while Grand Coulee was still being finished, and people of the upper river held a gathering at the falls that summer to mark the loss, remembered as the Ceremony of Tears.
